subject: english
question: Your group says, “We reckon the shady spot is best.” You are reporting its decision to the whole class. Which version keeps the idea and suits the report?
audio_prompt: Your group says, “We reckon the shady spot is best.” You are reporting its decision to the whole class. Which version keeps the idea and suits the report?

answers.text: Our group recommends the shaded area.
I recommend the shaded area.
We reckon that bit is the best one.
Our group has not chosen an area.

explanation.summary: The report names the group and its recommendation clearly. It keeps the shared decision, rather than changing it into one person’s view.
explanation.hint: Keep who decided and what they decided.

subject: english
question: You ask a close friend to pass a pencil during quiet partner work. Which request is relaxed and respectful?
audio_prompt: You ask a close friend to pass a pencil during quiet partner work. Which request is relaxed and respectful?

answers.text: I hereby request the transfer of the pencil.
Pass me the pencil, please.
You must give me your pencil immediately.
Dear class representative, please provide stationery.

explanation.summary: A short request with please suits familiar partners. Informal language can still be respectful.
explanation.hint: Consider how well these partners know each other.

subject: english
question: You are emailing a school office you have never contacted. Which opening clearly names your request without sounding like a message to a close friend?
audio_prompt: You are emailing a school office you have never contacted. Which opening clearly names your request without sounding like a message to a close friend?

answers.text: Hiya! When’s that thing happening?
Hello, I will tell you when library club starts.
Hello, could you tell me when library club starts?
Hey bestie, can you sort club stuff?

explanation.summary: The chosen opening is courteous and names library club. Formality supports a clear request; it does not require difficult words.
explanation.hint: Name the event and make the request clear.

subject: english
question: A group note says, “We picked blue because you can read it easily.” Which report sentence preserves both the choice and reason?
audio_prompt: A group note says, “We picked blue because you can read it easily.” Which report sentence preserves both the choice and reason?

answers.text: We chose blue because everyone likes it.
Blue is the only colour that anyone can read.
I chose blue, although our group wanted red.
We chose blue because the writing is easy to read.

explanation.summary: The report retains the group’s choice and its readability reason. More formal wording must not invent a reason or change the decision.
explanation.hint: Check the reason as well as the colour.

subject: english
question: A friend writes, “Want to join our game?” A club organiser writes, “Would you like to join the next club session?” What makes both invitations suitable?
audio_prompt: A friend writes, “Want to join our game?” A club organiser writes, “Would you like to join the next club session?” What makes both invitations suitable?

answers.text: Each uses a respectful invitation that fits its audience.
Only the second is respectful because it is longer.
The first is formal because it has a question mark.
Both must use the same greeting to be respectful.

explanation.summary: A familiar friend can use a shorter invitation. The organiser gives the session detail; neither needs to order the reader to attend.
explanation.hint: Separate formality from respect.

subject: english
question: In a report for families, replace “The stall made heaps of money” with wording that uses the supplied total of $85. Which version is precise?
audio_prompt: In a report for families, replace “The stall made heaps of money” with wording that uses the supplied total of $85. Which version is precise?

answers.text: The stall raised a fantastic fortune.
The stall raised $85.
The stall raised quite a lot.
The stall raised more than every other stall.

explanation.summary: The exact supplied amount replaces vague conversational wording without adding an unsupported comparison.
explanation.hint: Use the amount you were given.

subject: english
question: You are introducing a group project to visitors who have not seen it. Which opening helps them understand the topic?
audio_prompt: You are introducing a group project to visitors who have not seen it. Which opening helps them understand the topic?

answers.text: So, this is what we were talking about before.
You already know what our thing is about.
Our project compares two ways to save water at school.
As I said to Sam, that one worked.

explanation.summary: Visitors need the topic stated because they do not share the group’s earlier conversation.
explanation.hint: Ask what a new listener needs to know.

subject: english
question: A teacher writes, “I’m looking forward to hearing your ideas.” A student says the contraction makes the message rude. Which reply fits the example?
audio_prompt: A teacher writes, “I’m looking forward to hearing your ideas.” A student says the contraction makes the message rude. Which reply fits the example?

answers.text: Every contraction makes a message rude.
The message is rude because it mentions the teacher.
Removing the apostrophe would make it more respectful.
I’m is a contraction, but the message still welcomes ideas respectfully.

explanation.summary: Contractions can make language conversational; they do not automatically make it rude. The whole message and relationship matter.
explanation.hint: Read the invitation, not just one shortened word.

subject: english
question: During a game you captain, you say, “Please line up behind the cone.” Later you ask a teacher, “Could you help us check the rule?” Why does your language change?
audio_prompt: During a game you captain, you say, “Please line up behind the cone.” Later you ask a teacher, “Could you help us check the rule?” Why does your language change?

answers.text: Your role and purpose change from giving directions to asking for help.
You can be respectful only when you are the captain.
Questions are always informal and directions always formal.
The teacher must receive the longest possible sentence.

explanation.summary: A captain needs clear directions; a learner asks for help. Both can communicate respectfully.
explanation.hint: Compare what you are trying to do each time.

subject: english
question: Ten-year-old Lin has used the class camera often. Her older cousin is trying it for the first time. Which question recognises Lin’s experience?
audio_prompt: Ten-year-old Lin has used the class camera often. Her older cousin is trying it for the first time. Which question recognises Lin’s experience?

answers.text: Could the oldest person explain it, even if they have never used it?
Lin, could you show us how to focus this camera?
Lin, you are too young to help with the camera.
Can we skip instructions because the cousin is older?

explanation.summary: Experience with the camera matters here. Expertise is knowledge or skill, and it is not decided by age alone.
explanation.hint: Who knows how this particular tool works?

subject: english
question: Your friend Sam is leading your group’s presentation rehearsal. Which response respects both your friendship and Sam’s role?
audio_prompt: Your friend Sam is leading your group’s presentation rehearsal. Which response respects both your friendship and Sam’s role?

answers.text: You’re my friend, so your directions do not count.
Dear Sir or Madam, I formally demand a rehearsal.
Sam, could we practise the introduction once more?
I will talk over your instructions because I know you.

explanation.summary: A friendly, specific request recognises Sam’s role without pretending the friendship has disappeared.
explanation.hint: Keep friendliness and cooperation together.

subject: english
question: A younger child asks where the art room is. Which answer is clear without talking down to them?
audio_prompt: A younger child asks where the art room is. Which answer is clear without talking down to them?

answers.text: Locate the designated creative-arts facility adjacent to the library.
You are little, so you probably cannot find it.
You should already know where it is.
It is beside the library. I can point it out on the map.

explanation.summary: Simple landmarks and an offered map support understanding without judging the child’s ability.
explanation.hint: Choose clarity without an insult.

subject: english
question: Your swimming instructor asks everyone to use the name Alex. Which greeting follows this stated preference?
audio_prompt: Your swimming instructor asks everyone to use the name Alex. Which greeting follows this stated preference?

answers.text: Hello, Alex.
Hello, Mr Alex, because adults must always have a title.
Hello, Coach Smith, even though that is not the name given.
Hello, Sir, because preferences do not matter.

explanation.summary: Following a person’s stated name preference supports a respectful relationship. There is no need to invent a title.
explanation.hint: Use the preference actually supplied.

subject: english
question: Two families have different ways of greeting visitors. What could you ask respectfully before visiting a family you do not know well?
audio_prompt: Two families have different ways of greeting visitors. What could you ask respectfully before visiting a family you do not know well?

answers.text: Why does your family greet people the wrong way?
Is there a greeting or name you would like me to use?
Will everyone copy my family’s greeting?
Should I guess that all families use the same greeting?

explanation.summary: An open question lets people explain their preference without labelling one family’s convention as wrong.
explanation.hint: Allow for different conventions.

subject: english
question: You need help from an unfamiliar librarian. Which request gives enough information politely?
audio_prompt: You need help from an unfamiliar librarian. Which request gives enough information politely?

answers.text: Could you help me find that one?
Give me the book I am thinking of, please.
Excuse me, could you help me find a book about frogs?
You know the book, so bring it here.

explanation.summary: The request names the subject instead of assuming the librarian knows what you mean. Courtesy and useful detail work together.
explanation.hint: Does the listener know which book you mean?

subject: english
question: A guest expert says, “Please ask me if a word is unfamiliar.” You do not understand habitat. Which response follows the invitation?
audio_prompt: A guest expert says, “Please ask me if a word is unfamiliar.” You do not understand habitat. Which response follows the invitation?

answers.text: I will pretend I understand so that I sound polite.
You must stop using all new words.
Everyone knows that word, so I cannot ask.
Could you explain what habitat means, please?

explanation.summary: Asking for an explanation uses the expert’s invitation and helps you learn. Respect does not require pretending to understand.
explanation.hint: The speaker has invited a question.

subject: english
question: Your group invitation says, “Only good readers can help with our display.” Which revision includes different useful contributions?
audio_prompt: Your group invitation says, “Only good readers can help with our display.” Which revision includes different useful contributions?

answers.text: Everyone can help by reading, drawing, arranging or sharing ideas.
Only the fastest readers can decide who helps.
Everyone may watch while the good readers do everything.
Only people who read aloud without mistakes can join.

explanation.summary: Offering several meaningful ways to contribute welcomes classmates with different strengths. Watching alone is not the same as being offered a role.
explanation.hint: Look for real opportunities to contribute.

subject: english
question: At a group meeting, Noor has not spoken yet. Which invitation gives Noor a choice without putting them down?
audio_prompt: At a group meeting, Noor has not spoken yet. Which invitation gives Noor a choice without putting them down?

answers.text: Noor, you never have ideas, so speak now.
Noor, would you like to add an idea, or have a little more thinking time?
Everyone has spoken except you, so hurry.
We have decided you do not want a turn.

explanation.summary: A choice of contributing or thinking longer includes Noor without forcing or making assumptions.
explanation.hint: Invite rather than pressure.

subject: english
question: A notice says, “Bring your mum and dad to the reading afternoon.” Which change welcomes different family arrangements?
audio_prompt: A notice says, “Bring your mum and dad to the reading afternoon.” Which change welcomes different family arrangements?

answers.text: Bring the same two adults as everyone else.
Bring only a parent who lives with you.
Bring a family member or carer to the reading afternoon.
Bring both parents or do not attend.

explanation.summary: Family member or carer includes more kinds of caring relationships without requiring every home to be the same.
explanation.hint: Think about who may care for a child.

subject: english
question: The class is choosing jobs for a play. Which sentence avoids deciding roles from gender?
audio_prompt: The class is choosing jobs for a play. Which sentence avoids deciding roles from gender?

answers.text: Boys must move props and girls must make costumes.
Girls can suggest ideas after boys choose their jobs.
Only boys should speak the narrator’s part.
Choose a job you are interested in, and we will share the roles fairly.

explanation.summary: Interest and fair sharing provide access to roles without a gender rule.
explanation.hint: Is any group excluded before choosing?

subject: english
question: A classmate’s name is unfamiliar to you. Which response helps you use it respectfully?
audio_prompt: A classmate’s name is unfamiliar to you. Which response helps you use it respectfully?

answers.text: Could you say your name for me so I can practise saying it correctly?
I will shorten your name because it is new to me.
Everyone should use a name I already know.
I will avoid speaking to you until I learn it.

explanation.summary: Asking and practising shows care without changing someone’s name for your convenience.
explanation.hint: Let the person guide their own name.

subject: english
question: Your team says, “That is a stupid idea.” Which revision disagrees with the idea while keeping discussion open?
audio_prompt: Your team says, “That is a stupid idea.” Which revision disagrees with the idea while keeping discussion open?

answers.text: That idea is still stupid, but please listen.
I am worried the bridge will bend. Could we add a support?
You always get building ideas wrong.
We should never hear your suggestions again.

explanation.summary: The revision identifies a concern and proposes a change. It does not attack the person.
explanation.hint: Name the concern, not an insult.

subject: english
question: A group leader says, “We all agree,” but two members have not been asked. Which sentence is more inclusive and accurate?
audio_prompt: A group leader says, “We all agree,” but two members have not been asked. Which sentence is more inclusive and accurate?

answers.text: We all agree because I have chosen.
The quiet members definitely agree.
We have heard two views. What do the others think?
We can count silence as a yes every time.

explanation.summary: Asking for other views avoids claiming agreement that has not been checked.
explanation.hint: Silence does not tell you everyone’s view.

subject: english
question: A new classmate says they do not know the rules of your game. Which invitation helps them join?
audio_prompt: A new classmate says they do not know the rules of your game. Which invitation helps them join?

answers.text: You can join only after learning the rules alone.
You may watch because everyone else already knows.
We will use harder words so that you learn faster.
Would you like us to explain the rules and try a practice round with you?

explanation.summary: An explanation and practice round offer practical support and a genuine invitation.
explanation.hint: Include the person in the activity, not just the space.

subject: english
question: Your teacher is arranging a visit from a First Nations Elder. The visitor has not yet given a preferred name or greeting. What should the class ask the teacher to check?
audio_prompt: Your teacher is arranging a visit from a First Nations Elder. The visitor has not yet given a preferred name or greeting. What should the class ask the teacher to check?

answers.text: The visitor’s preferred form of address and appropriate local greeting guidance.
Which title every First Nations Elder must use.
A greeting from any community to use everywhere.
Whether guessing a title is quicker than asking.

explanation.summary: The teacher should consult the visitor and appropriate local guidance. A respectful form of address must not be assumed from a general rule.
explanation.hint: Check preferences rather than inventing a universal rule.

subject: english
question: A visiting Elder has told your teacher, “Please call me Aunty Jo.” Which greeting follows this particular invitation?
audio_prompt: A visiting Elder has told your teacher, “Please call me Aunty Jo.” Which greeting follows this particular invitation?

answers.text: Welcome, Jo, because I never use invited titles.
Welcome, Aunty Jo. Thank you for visiting our class.
Welcome, Aunty, because every visitor must have that title.
Welcome, Mrs Jo, because I prefer a different title.

explanation.summary: Aunty Jo is appropriate here because this visitor invited that form of address. The example does not create a rule for all Elders.
explanation.hint: Use the stated invitation only for this situation.

subject: english
question: A class has read an approved account of greetings in one First Nations community. Which conclusion stays within that evidence?
audio_prompt: A class has read an approved account of greetings in one First Nations community. Which conclusion stays within that evidence?

answers.text: Every First Nations community must greet people this way.
The account gives permission to invent new traditional greetings.
The account describes that community; other communities may have different conventions.
One account means there is no need for local guidance.

explanation.summary: One community’s account cannot stand for every First Nations community. Keep the source and its scope clear.
explanation.hint: Ask whose convention the source describes.

subject: english
question: Before recording a guest’s explanation of a greeting, what is the respectful next step?
audio_prompt: Before recording a guest’s explanation of a greeting, what is the respectful next step?

answers.text: Record first because it is for school.
Record secretly so nobody feels interrupted.
Assume speaking to a class allows public sharing.
Ask whether recording is permitted and follow any limits the guest gives.

explanation.summary: Permission to speak with a class is not automatically permission to record or share. Follow the guest’s decision.
explanation.hint: Speaking, recording and sharing are separate permissions.

subject: english
question: A teacher says local greeting conventions will be explained by an invited knowledge holder. Which preparation respects that plan?
audio_prompt: A teacher says local greeting conventions will be explained by an invited knowledge holder. Which preparation respects that plan?

answers.text: Prepare a question about how to greet respectfully, then listen to the local guidance.
Practise a made-up traditional greeting and call it local.
Choose one greeting online and insist the guest use it.
Assume all First Nations Australians greet one another identically.

explanation.summary: A prepared question supports learning from the invited person. It does not invent or generalise cultural knowledge.
explanation.hint: Learn from the named source rather than guessing.

subject: english
question: During a visitor’s talk, a student listens without making constant eye contact. What should the class avoid assuming?
audio_prompt: During a visitor’s talk, a student listens without making constant eye contact. What should the class avoid assuming?

answers.text: That listening can include paying attention to the words.
That this alone proves the student is disrespectful.
That people can have different non-verbal conventions.
That the teacher can explain agreed discussion expectations.

explanation.summary: Eye-contact conventions differ, and one behaviour alone does not establish disrespect. Look for attentive, considerate participation without a universal eye-contact rule.
explanation.hint: Do not judge respect from one gesture alone.

subject: english
question: A formal note says, “Please return the library book by Friday.” A student replaces it with “Please return the item sometime.” What was lost?
audio_prompt: A formal note says, “Please return the library book by Friday.” A student replaces it with “Please return the item sometime.” What was lost?

answers.text: A necessary insult to the reader.
The only polite word in the sentence.
The precise object and deadline.
A rule that all notes must be long.

explanation.summary: The revision becomes vague: item and sometime do not preserve library book and Friday. Formal communication still needs precise meaning.
explanation.hint: Compare the information in the two versions.

subject: english
question: You want to ask a friend for help, not order them. Which small change makes “Help me with this puzzle” clearly a request with a choice?
audio_prompt: You want to ask a friend for help, not order them. Which small change makes “Help me with this puzzle” clearly a request with a choice?

answers.text: Help me with this puzzle immediately.
You have to help me with this puzzle.
You will help me with this puzzle now.
Could you help me with this puzzle?

explanation.summary: Could you turns the instruction into a request. A familiar friendship does not remove the other person’s choice.
explanation.hint: Look at the kind of sentence, not its length.

subject: english
question: For a visitor report, Lee changes “Our plant went bananas” to “Our plant grew 6 cm this week.” Why is the change useful if the measurement is supplied?
audio_prompt: For a visitor report, Lee changes “Our plant went bananas” to “Our plant grew 6 cm this week.” Why is the change useful if the measurement is supplied?

answers.text: It replaces an idiom with a clear measured change.
It proves every idiom is rude.
It changes the plant into a different species.
It makes the report less precise.

explanation.summary: The measured change is easier for this audience to interpret. An idiom can be suitable elsewhere; this task needs clarity.
explanation.hint: Choose the explanation that fits this report.

subject: english
question: Your team wants to suggest a different game rule. Which sentence gives a reason and invites discussion?
audio_prompt: Your team wants to suggest a different game rule. Which sentence gives a reason and invites discussion?

answers.text: We must change it because I always decide.
Could we allow another turn so everyone gets a chance?
You have to accept my rule without discussing it.
We should ignore anyone who likes the old rule.

explanation.summary: The proposal explains its inclusive purpose and invites rather than demands agreement.
explanation.hint: Look for a reason and space for another view.

subject: english
question: An unfamiliar adult and your close friend both ask about your model. Which fact helps you choose how much explanation to give?
audio_prompt: An unfamiliar adult and your close friend both ask about your model. Which fact helps you choose how much explanation to give?

answers.text: Only which person is older.
Only which person speaks louder.
Whether each listener already knows how the model works.
Whether you can use the longest words you know.

explanation.summary: Familiarity with the topic affects the detail needed. Age alone cannot tell you what someone knows.
explanation.hint: Consider the listener’s existing knowledge.

subject: english
question: A class poster says, “Ask if you need help; you can speak, write or point to your choice.” How can this wording support participation?
audio_prompt: A class poster says, “Ask if you need help; you can speak, write or point to your choice.” How can this wording support participation?

answers.text: It requires everyone to speak in the same way.
It guarantees that every task is now easy for everyone.
It says only written answers count.
It offers different ways to communicate a choice.

explanation.summary: Offering options can help different learners participate. It does not guarantee that no further support will be needed.
explanation.hint: Notice what the poster actually offers.

subject: english
question: You want to borrow coloured paper. Write one request to a close friend and one to the unfamiliar school office assistant. Keep the request the same and explain one wording change.
audio_prompt: You want to borrow coloured paper. Write one request to a close friend and one to the unfamiliar school office assistant. Keep the request the same and explain one wording change.
model_answer: Friend: “Could I borrow some coloured paper, please?” Office: “Hello, could you please tell me whether I may borrow some coloured paper?” I added a greeting and fuller request for someone I do not know.
acceptance_note: Check two suitable requests for the same paper, a defensible difference for the relationships and an explanation. Accept respectful natural alternatives; do not require slang or complicated words.
response_instructions: Complete the actual task in writing, aloud with an adult, or using your usual communication support. An adult checks the completed evidence against the guidance.
completion_label: My completed work is ready for an adult to check.

explanation.summary: Friend: “Could I borrow some coloured paper, please?” Office: “Hello, could you please tell me whether I may borrow some coloured paper?” I added a greeting and fuller request for someone I do not know.
explanation.hint: Name the audience before choosing the wording.

subject: english
question: Your group says, “We chose the corner by the window. There’s more light there.” Write two sentences for your group’s report to the class, then underline a change that helps the audience.
audio_prompt: Your group says, “We chose the corner by the window. There’s more light there.” Write two sentences for your group’s report to the class, then underline a change that helps the audience.
model_answer: “Our group chose the corner beside the window. This location has more light.” The report names the group and location clearly.
acceptance_note: Require the group decision, window location and light reason to remain unchanged, plus an identified audience-helping change. Do not accept an invented measurement.
response_instructions: Complete the actual task in writing, aloud with an adult, or using your usual communication support. An adult checks the completed evidence against the guidance.
completion_label: My completed work is ready for an adult to check.

explanation.summary: “Our group chose the corner beside the window. This location has more light.” The report names the group and location clearly.
explanation.hint: Preserve the decision and its reason.

subject: english
question: With an adult or class partner, rehearse a request to join a familiar friend’s game and a request to join an unfamiliar organised club activity. Say both versions and explain how they suit each listener. You may use writing or your usual communication support.
audio_prompt: With an adult or class partner, rehearse a request to join a familiar friend’s game and a request to join an unfamiliar organised club activity. Say both versions and explain how they suit each listener. You may use writing or your usual communication support.
model_answer: Friend: “Is there room for me to join?” Organiser: “Hello, could you tell me how I can join this activity?” The second names the purpose for an unfamiliar organiser.
acceptance_note: Observe both actual messages and an explanation of one audience-related choice. Accept writing or usual communication supports. Do not judge accent, eye contact or confidence as respect.
response_instructions: Complete the actual task in writing, aloud with an adult, or using your usual communication support. An adult checks the completed evidence against the guidance.
completion_label: My completed work is ready for an adult to check.

explanation.summary: Friend: “Is there room for me to join?” Organiser: “Hello, could you tell me how I can join this activity?” The second names the purpose for an unfamiliar organiser.
explanation.hint: Try a greeting, clear request and considerate tone.

subject: english
question: A nine-year-old has learned to use the school telescope; an older visitor is new to it. Write a question that recognises the child’s expertise and explain why you chose to ask them.
audio_prompt: A nine-year-old has learned to use the school telescope; an older visitor is new to it. Write a question that recognises the child’s expertise and explain why you chose to ask them.
model_answer: “Could you show me how to focus this telescope?” I asked the child because they have practised using it, not because they are older.
acceptance_note: Check a respectful relevant question and an explanation based on telescope experience rather than age alone.
response_instructions: Complete the actual task in writing, aloud with an adult, or using your usual communication support. An adult checks the completed evidence against the guidance.
completion_label: My completed work is ready for an adult to check.

explanation.summary: “Could you show me how to focus this telescope?” I asked the child because they have practised using it, not because they are older.
explanation.hint: Think about who has the useful knowledge.

subject: english
question: Revise this invitation so different classmates can contribute: “Only people who are good at drawing can help make our welcome sign.” Give at least two useful ways to help and explain your change.
audio_prompt: Revise this invitation so different classmates can contribute: “Only people who are good at drawing can help make our welcome sign.” Give at least two useful ways to help and explain your change.
model_answer: “Everyone can help our welcome sign by drawing, choosing words or arranging letters.” The invitation includes different strengths.
acceptance_note: Require a genuine invitation, at least two meaningful contributions and an explanation of inclusion. Watching alone is not a useful role unless chosen by that student.
response_instructions: Complete the actual task in writing, aloud with an adult, or using your usual communication support. An adult checks the completed evidence against the guidance.
completion_label: My completed work is ready for an adult to check.

explanation.summary: “Everyone can help our welcome sign by drawing, choosing words or arranging letters.” The invitation includes different strengths.
explanation.hint: Offer roles rather than label people as good or bad.

subject: english
question: Your group says, “We all want a running game,” but one member has asked for a quieter choice. Write a response that acknowledges that person and helps the group discuss an inclusive option.
audio_prompt: Your group says, “We all want a running game,” but one member has asked for a quieter choice. Write a response that acknowledges that person and helps the group discuss an inclusive option.
model_answer: “We have heard a request for a quieter game. Could we choose a game with active and quiet roles, or discuss another idea together?”
acceptance_note: Check acknowledgment of the actual request and an open practical discussion. Do not require one particular game or speak for everyone without asking.
response_instructions: Complete the actual task in writing, aloud with an adult, or using your usual communication support. An adult checks the completed evidence against the guidance.
completion_label: My completed work is ready for an adult to check.

explanation.summary: “We have heard a request for a quieter game. Could we choose a game with active and quiet roles, or discuss another idea together?”
explanation.hint: Show that you heard the other person.

subject: english
question: A teammate wants to use a tall cardboard tower, but you think it may fall. Write a two-line conversation: explain your concern respectfully, then give a reply that invites a shared solution.
audio_prompt: A teammate wants to use a tall cardboard tower, but you think it may fall. Write a two-line conversation: explain your concern respectfully, then give a reply that invites a shared solution.
model_answer: “I’m worried the tower may fall. Could we widen its base?” “Let’s try that and check whether it stands.”
acceptance_note: Require a specific concern, no personal insult, and a reply that supports a joint next step. Accept other reasonable solutions.
response_instructions: Complete the actual task in writing, aloud with an adult, or using your usual communication support. An adult checks the completed evidence against the guidance.
completion_label: My completed work is ready for an adult to check.

explanation.summary: “I’m worried the tower may fall. Could we widen its base?” “Let’s try that and check whether it stands.”
explanation.hint: Discuss the tower, not the person’s ability.

subject: english
question: Before a First Nations Elder’s class visit, write two questions for the teacher to check with the visitor: one about preferred address or greetings and one about permission to record or share. Do not invent the visitor’s answers.
audio_prompt: Before a First Nations Elder’s class visit, write two questions for the teacher to check with the visitor: one about preferred address or greetings and one about permission to record or share. Do not invent the visitor’s answers.
model_answer: “What name or form of address would the visitor like us to use?” “May we record or share any part of the visit, and what limits should we follow?”
acceptance_note: Require two distinct respectful checks and no invented answers or universal cultural rule. The teacher should consult the visitor and appropriate local guidance.
response_instructions: Complete the actual task in writing, aloud with an adult, or using your usual communication support. An adult checks the completed evidence against the guidance.
completion_label: My completed work is ready for an adult to check.

explanation.summary: “What name or form of address would the visitor like us to use?” “May we record or share any part of the visit, and what limits should we follow?”
explanation.hint: Ask what you do not yet know.

subject: english
question: A classmate says, “We read one community’s greeting account, so we know how every First Nations community greets.” Write a respectful correction and a useful next learning step.
audio_prompt: A classmate says, “We read one community’s greeting account, so we know how every First Nations community greets.” Write a respectful correction and a useful next learning step.
model_answer: “That account describes one community, not every community. We can ask our teacher for locally endorsed guidance and keep the source’s name with our notes.”
acceptance_note: Check a clear limit on the generalisation and a respectful source-led next step. No invented language or greeting is needed.
response_instructions: Complete the actual task in writing, aloud with an adult, or using your usual communication support. An adult checks the completed evidence against the guidance.
completion_label: My completed work is ready for an adult to check.

explanation.summary: “That account describes one community, not every community. We can ask our teacher for locally endorsed guidance and keep the source’s name with our notes.”
explanation.hint: Keep the community and source visible.

question: Write a short note inviting a close friend to help pack books. Then adapt it for an unfamiliar community volunteer. Keep the task unchanged and explain why a longer message is not automatically better.

question: Your group discussed a garden: “Let’s put the herbs near the tap so watering’s easier.” Which sentence suits a class report without changing the proposal?

question: A school invitation says, “Ask a parent or carer to help you prepare.” Why is this more inclusive than requiring every child’s father to help?
